title: The Sun's 'Switch-Off' Signal That Forecasts the Next Cycle
hook: Partway through the Sun's 11-year cycle, a 'switch-off' moment shuts down its most violent storms — and the sunspots left over forecast the next cycle's strength years in advance.
key_points: Solar activity runs on an ~11-year cycle, but predicting the next cycle's strength usually meant waiting for solar minimum to arrive.
Researchers found a 'switch-off' point: when active sunspot regions drift below about 15° latitude, the driver of violent space weather weakens and the worst storms end abruptly.
The number of sunspots present at switch-off closely tracks the peak sunspot count of the following cycle.
That link gives roughly six to seven years' advance warning of a new cycle's strength.
Early projections put the coming Solar Cycle 26 at a moderate ~100-120 sunspots, similar to or weaker than the current cycle.
content_html: The Sun runs on an roughly 11-year rhythm, swinging from quiet to storm-tossed and back. Forecasting how fierce the next swing will be has traditionally meant waiting for solar minimum — the lull between cycles — before making a call, which leaves little time to prepare for space weather that can disrupt satellites and power grids.
extra_html: Professor Sandra Chapman of the University of Warwick's Centre for Fusion, Space and Astrophysics identified an earlier tell: a "switch-off" point midway through the cycle. As a cycle's active sunspot regions migrate toward the equator and drop below about 15 degrees of solar latitude, the differential rotation that normally twists up the Sun's magnetic field weakens. Since that twisting is what powers the biggest coronal mass ejections, the most violent space weather shuts off relatively abruptly. The useful part: the number of sunspots present at that switch-off moment closely tracks the peak the following cycle will reach, handing forecasters roughly six to seven years' notice instead of waiting for minimum. Applied to what's coming, early projections point to a moderate Solar Cycle 26 of about 100 to 120 sunspots — similar to, or a bit weaker than, the current cycle — with a sharper forecast expected in about two years. Presented at the Royal Astronomical Society's National Astronomy Meeting.

related.title: What Powers the Sun
related.hook: The Sun isn't burning like a fire — it's fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, and a sliver of mass turning into pure energy is what lights up our sky.

related.title: Why the Solar Wind Hits the Moon's Two Sides Differently
related.hook: The Moon's near and far hemispheres soak up the solar wind unequally — because Earth's own magnetic shield shadows the near side. Chang'e-6's far-side dirt caught the difference.

flashcards.back_html: Active sunspot regions drift below about 15° solar latitude, weakening the twisting of magnetic fields that drives coronal mass ejections — so the most violent space weather ends abruptly.
